A Russian air attack on Zaporizhzhia in Ukraine has killed two people and wounded more than 40, including an infant, the day after Kyiv said its drones sank a Russian warship in a Libyan port far from the front lines of the war.

Russia’s dawn raid on the city in southeast Ukraine destroyed a house and damaged a five-storey apartment building, regional officials said on Tuesday.

- list 2 of 3What Russian warship did Ukraine just sink?
- list 3 of 3Russia threatens ‘hostile’ Estonia with ‘open war’

It came as the two warring sides continued long-range attacks, launching hundreds of drones overnight.

Russia’s Ministry of Defence said air defences intercepted and destroyed 699 Ukrainian drones over seven regions, occupied Crimea and the Black Sea.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 355 drones flew towards the capital overnight and 63 were shot down as they approached.

Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Amin Dorghami said it had been a “long time” since Moscow had been targeted with as many drones.

Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 96 drones overnight, with hits at 13 locations and 73 shot down or jammed.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces hit an electricity substation in Pryluky, in Ukraine’s Chernihiv region, which it said powered Ukraine’s military. Russian forces also hit a dry cargo ship southwest of Odesa that the ministry said was carrying military supplies.

“This too could be considered routine, since Russia is enforcing a blockade on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports,” Dorghami said.

Late on Monday, the Polish military said a Russian drone briefly entered Poland’s airspace during an attack on western Ukraine but was not shot down because of the risk to civilians. Deputy Defence Minister Pawel Zalewski said he assumed the incursion was deliberate, coming three days after three Russian cruise missiles crashed in eastern Poland.

Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Abdelaziz Mujahid said the incursion “may also signal that the conflict and these confrontations are widening”.

It follows Ukraine’s attack on the Russian corvette Merkury in the Libyan port of Benghazi on Sunday. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said seven Ukrainian-built naval drones were used in the “completely legitimate operation against enemy ships”.

“The strike in Benghazi has left Russia without one of its newest combat ships,” said Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow. “It was commissioned only three years ago.”

Russia’s UN envoy, Vassily Nebenzia, accused Western countries of backing Ukraine’s recent attacks and said Moscow would keep using military means to ensure its security.

On Monday, debris from Russian drones fell in central Kyiv, close to the president’s office and set a five-storey building on fire. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people were injured, including a foreign national.

“All of this is a bit too close for comfort for Ukrainians, especially considering that the presidential palace is just a few hundred metres up the road,” reported Al Jazeera’s Audrey McAlpine from the scene.

Zelenskyy said on Monday evening that Ukrainian intelligence warned that Russia was preparing a new series of strikes and urged residents to heed air raid alerts.

**A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to the UK, where he was set to attend a series of events.**

Saurav Das said he was supposed to board a flight on Tuesday at 01:00 local time (19:30 GMT on Monday) but was told by immigration officers that his passport had been "flagged".

It is not clear yet why Das's passport was flagged. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.

Das, who rose to prominence in India earlier this year after Gen Z-led protests, said that he had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about the movement.

He said that he was also scheduled to speak at other universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh.

"Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual [government] was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions," Das wrote on X.

A federal home ministry spokesperson directed the BBC to airport authorities and the Delhi police for comment on Das's allegations.

On Tuesday, the London School of Economics Student Union's Amnesty International Unit, a student-led charity group, shared a post on Instagram saying that an event featuring Das had been "indefinitely postponed".

Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said in a post on X that she and Das had been invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected a few days ago.

"The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country," she wrote.

Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.

In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .

In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands of people detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.

The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.

There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.

In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.

In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.

**Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.**

Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.

The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.

But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule. She denies the charges.

Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms.

"Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.

Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.

India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In April, the ministry said it was examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties".

Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.

What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.

On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution.

"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said in a statement.

The choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement.

Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh.

Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile.

The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster.

The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister.

But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return.

Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so.

"I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster.

Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka.

India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a new government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster.

But nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September.

Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi.

The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.
texts.7aebfbd15f75:
A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying for a foreign country, a government-linked publisher has said.

Gold Wall Press, a publishing company associated with China’s national administration of state secrets protection, said the convicted person was surnamed Ma and was approached and recruited by an unnamed foreign intelligence service while working abroad.

Chinese courts typically do not publish information about state security cases, but in recent years the powerful ministry of state security and Gold Wall Press have increasingly publicised arrests, as well as using social media, movies and comics to promote warnings about espionage.

The statement on Monday said Ma had signed a cooperation agreement containing clauses on “confidentiality” and “loyalty” and received fixed monthly payments. In total, it said, he provided 35 pieces of information that were classified as national secrets and received payments worth more than 1m yuan ($150,000).

An intelligence operative identified as Kailin “frequently arranged to meet with Ma, hoping to engage with him more”, citing an interest in learning Chinese, the statement said. Kailin later introduced him to a colleague who threatened to report his earlier disclosures to Chinese authorities if he refused to cooperate.

After returning to China, Ma continued to gather intelligence for the foreign agency, which provided him with a laptop, the statement said. He used his position to collect material from classified documents during the day and transmitted it overseas at night via an espionage website.

The statement did not identify the countries involved, or say when or where he was sentenced or whether he had already been executed.

The case comes as US intelligence has been publicising its own efforts to recruit sources in China. The five most-viewed videos on the CIA’s YouTube channel are recruiting advertisements in Mandarin.

“This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call,” the Gold Wall Press said, warning that foreign intelligence agencies were “cunning” and used emotional ties, financial interests and threats to recruit people in key positions.

The statement also urged officials to remain vigilant, strengthen their loyalty to the Communist party, protect state secrets and guard against foreign recruitment.

In 2023 Beijing broadened its anti-espionage law, expanding the definition of espionage and strengthening the investigative powers of state security authorities. The following year it revised its state secrets law to extend restrictions on sensitive information to so-called “work secrets”.

**Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li**
texts.9c628f0a3100:
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.

After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.

The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported.

## How passive investing is fueling the AI trade

The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors.

Yet, those seeking a safe haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter.

Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors.

These indices have become increasingly exposed to the AI boom.

## Riding the winners works — until it doesn't

Most flagship index funds are keen to ride winners, so they automatically buy stocks according to a company's market value. The bigger a company grows, the more of it they hold.

The values of Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other US technology giants have benefited from this effect, with many soaring after ChatGPT was first released in late 2022.

The US also has an outsized position in funds that track the global economy. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), an index of more than 2,400 firms across 47 developed and emerging markets, are US Big Tech names.

The other is TSMC, a Taiwanese chipmaker that produces 90% of the high-end AI semiconductors.

Together, these 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index.

Although it's a global index, nearly two-thirds of MSCI ACWI's value is in US-listed companies, even though they make up only around a fifth of its firms.

## Don't put all your chips in AI stocks

"A well-diversified portfolio should ... reasonably represent the entire global economy," Gerd Kommer, founder of the Munich-based asset manager Gerd Kommer Invest, told DW.

"That's not the case if 70% of the portfolio is concentrated in just one country — the US. The global economy is more resilient than any national economy."

Kommer, who is known as Germany's "ETF pope," said investors need exposure to all economic sectors and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio.

Yet, even if investors want to avoid US-dominated World funds altogether, the AI trade still overshadows several other top index funds.

In MSCI's Emerging Market index, for example, the top 10 make up 37.5% of its value and TSMC alone accounts for almost 16%. Tech, chip and internet firms make up eight of the largest holdings, alongside two banks — one Chinese, one Indian.

## How funds fuel investor hubris

That matters, according to Dimitri Vayanos, a finance professor at the London School of Economics who studies how passive investing pushes up the prices of the biggest firms.

"My model suggests that the effects of flows into index funds are larger when the large stocks happen to be in the same industry," Vayanos told DW.

When some investors get over-optimistic about a company and push the stock price up, index funds add to that price pressure.

Professional investors then often bet against overpriced stocks, a practice known as "shorting," which helps pull prices back down. But that's far riskier with, say, a tech giant than with a small firm.

"Being short 1% of SpaceX involves much more risk than being short 1% of a small company," said Vayanos.

The problem gets worse when the biggest firms are all in the same sector, as they are now. As short-sellers hold back, the biggest stocks climb further, creating what he calls an "amplification-overpricing spiral."

## Lower AI risk outside of US, Asia

To cut exposure to AI-related stocks, investors may have to turn to developed market funds outside the US and Southeast Asia. These funds have offered lower returns over the past decade.

In the MSCI Europe, Australasia and Far East (EAFE) index fund, the top 10 holdings make up about 14.5% of the index, about 40% lower than the all-country world index.

EAFE's major holdings include healthcare giant Roche, oil major Shell, HSBC bank and Nestle — the world's largest food and beverage company.

However, its biggest holding, ASML, is still very much part of the AI trade. The Dutch tech firm sells the equipment that firms such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron need to make their chips.

## AI crash will have ripple effects

If Monday's rebound in the AI trade is sustained, stock prices may move sharply higher over the next few months. Yet if history is a guide, the bubble will eventually burst, leaving both institutional and passive investors nursing heavy losses.

Kommer warned that if the AI bubble bursts, "in all likelihood it will drag down the global stock market," though the damage would be most severe in tech and AI stocks.

Those hit hardest would be retail investors "with heavy portfolio weights in tech and AI stocks," he told DW, including "a lot of people who have bought individual AI-related stocks on top of their equity ETFs."

LSE's Vayanos thinks it is still "certainly safer to hold an ETF than to hold individual stocks."

But as index providers add mega-IPOs such as SpaceX and Claude-maker Anthropic to benchmarks within weeks of their debut, and money continues to pour into passive funds, he warned that "the conditions are present for the effects of our theory to be even stronger."
